Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Controlled desilication of porous silicates and zeolites is desirable for a range of industrial applications, including generation of mesoporous and hierarchical frameworks (1,2) for catalysis (3−8) and even the generation of novel zeolite frameworks. (9,10) It is well established that the extent of desilication is dependent on a number of factors, including silicon and water content. At high Si:Al ratios, zeolites are more susceptible to desilication, (11) while at low Si:Al ratios, dealumination is preferred both under steaming and acidic liquid water conditions. Another crucial factor in the rate and mechanism of zeolite decomposition is pH. Alkaline hydrolysis is selective for desilication over dealumination. (12) It has also been proposed that in high-silica zeolites, desilication may be initiated at internal silanol sites, which act as nucleation centers for reactive water. (13) In alkaline hydrolysis, it is not currently clear whether the increased desilication with pH is indicative of a change in the hydrolysis mechanism from neutral water hydrolysis or related to dissolution and reconstitution of the framework. Several authors have proposed explanations for the correlation between pH and the desilication rate, including: * Alkaline conditions removing the framework healing route (dehydroxylation) via deprotonation of reaction products. (14,15) * The introduction of hydrolysis mechanisms via OH– ions, with low reaction barriers. (16) * The presence of a spectator Na+ cation. (17) * The permanent loss of silicon via oligomerization after removal from the framework. (18) Owing to computational limitations, the majority of calculations on alkaline desilication have employed cluster models of silica in the absence of explicit solvent, with SN2-type mechanisms, which assume an attack of OH– on the framework. Such models have been useful to inform on possible reaction pathways (19) and to rationalize the significant enhancement in reaction rates with respect to neutral water hydrolysis. (20) However, the lack of explicit base molecules, solvent, and confinement effects remain a severe limitation to the accuracy of the models. Within the confined micropore volumes of zeolites, the maximum water content available to participate in hydrolysis reactions is low. For example, in zeolite chabazite (CHA), a water concentration of 1 g cm–1 corresponds to five molecules per cage, which is equivalent to only the first solvation shell of commonly present ions, such as Na+. Hence, the concept of microsolvation (21−25) is appropriate for describing the solvating environment within zeolites. Despite the small number of water molecules present, it has been shown that the local water concentration has a major effect on neutral silicate hydrolysis. Under conditions of low water concentration, the desilication pathway is established to proceed according to an equatorial mechanism with high energetic barriers. (20,26,27) By contrast, under higher water loading (>3 molecules at the reaction center), molecular chains are spontaneously formed between water molecules, which act as a Grotthuss-type proton transfer agent, driving a low-barrier hydrolysis mechanism. This has been observed both in molecular models of disiloxanes (20) and, more recently, in extended models of the interior of a zeolite pore. (28) Hence, the loading of water in the pore profoundly affects both the energetics and the mechanism of hydrolysis. Although pristine, siliceous zeolites are hydrophobic, defects, such as internal silanol nests and regions of incompletely condensed framework, can act as nucleation centers to draw in water. (13) Nearby Al sites also promote the incorporation of water into the pore. (29) In addition, under basic conditions, water is both the carrier of NaOH and is in excess. The sensitivity of the hydrolysis energetics and mechanism to water content therefore necessitates a careful study of the role of water in the desilication of siliceous zeolites under basic conditions. The high pH, which enhances silicate hydrolysis is caused by the presence of OH– generating species, such as NaOH. However, few studies have considered the role of NaOH in the process. Na cations are relatively bulky, with a first hydration shell of around five water molecules, (30) and are known to commonly occupy the face of six-ring sites in zeolites under anhydrous conditions. (31−33) Hence, the cation is likely to affect reaction mechanisms, either directly or as a water adsorption center. It has been reported that Na+ can stabilize activated Si complexes at quartz surfaces. (17) However, the possibility of NaOH to directly split siloxane bonds was not considered. Direct attack of NaOH has also been investigated on the surface of zeolite ZSM-5 in which a series of SN2 reactions replace framework Si–OSi bonds with Si–OH and SiO–Na+ species. (18) This mechanism neglects solvent and leads to a high consumption of reacting NaOH. Both such studies are focused on hydrolysis originating at the surface of the zeolite. There is, however, evidence for “inside-out” hydrolysis of zeolites, particularly originating at internal silanols. (13) There are currently no atomistic investigations, which correspond to explicit base-catalyzed hydrolysis from within the zeolite micropore. Furthermore, the coinclusion of base and solvent has not been attempted, despite likely synergies between NaOH and H2O. Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Global warming has been correlated to the increased concentration of greenhouse gases (GHGs) in the atmosphere caused by anthropogenic emissions since the beginning of the industrial age. (1) In the Paris Climate Agreement, 194 parties agreed to limit global warming to 2 °C (and more preferably 1.5 °C) above preindustrial levels. (2,3) In order to reach this goal, a decrease in anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and/or the removal of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere are considered crucial requirements. (2,4) Among all anthropogenic greenhouse gases present in the atmosphere, carbon dioxide (CO2) is the one with the highest concentration. (5) The major sources of CO2 emission are industrial plants, such as cement and ammonia plants, and thermoelectric power plants. (5) Although many efforts have been devoted to the development of cleaner, more renewable and environmentally safer production processes, most chemical and power plants still rely on fossil feedstock leading to CO2 emissions. Against this backdrop, increasing attention has been devoted to the mitigation of carbon dioxide emissions through carbon capture and storage (CCS) or carbon capture and utilization (CCU) technologies. (6−8) CCS is focused on the capture of CO2 from large point sources, such as power plants, so that it can be injected in the ground, for example in depleted oil and gas fields or in saline formations, for long-term storage. (9) CCU aims at a more sustainable and circular solution in which CO2 is employed directly, for example, as a solvent (10) or as a feedstock in the production of chemicals and synthetic fuels. (11,12) There are many processes generating CO2 emissions to which CCS or CCU can be applied, and for each specific process the CO2-containing stream varies in composition. In most processes, CO2 needs to be separated from other gases, such as N2, H2 or CH4. In power plants there are three approaches for CO2 capture, namely precombustion separation, postcombustion separation, and oxycombustion. Postcombustion capture is the capture of CO2 from flue gas (CO2/N2 separation) generated through the combustion of coal or natural gas with air in conventional power plants. (13) However, the CO2 concentration in flue gas is low (≤15 vol %), which makes the separation more difficult since the minimum thermodynamic work required for separation increases with decreasing CO2 concentration. (14) This results in a higher energy penalty for CO2 capture from low-concentration streams. Precombustion capture is used in integrated gasification combined cycle (IGCC) power plants, in which coal is thermally converted into syngas (CO/H2 mixture), which can be enriched in H2 through the water–gas shift reaction in which CO and H2O are converted into CO2 and H2. (13) CO2 is captured for storage or utilization such that H2 can be used as a fuel to produce electric power. In precombustion capture, the CO2 concentration is higher (>15 vol %) than for postcombustion capture and, therefore, the separation is less energy intensive. (14) However, this option is currently less common as this technology has started to be employed in power plants only recently. Oxycombustion is another alternative power plant design, in which pure O2 instead of air is used for combustion, which leads to a flue gas consisting predominantly of H2O and CO2. (15) However, high purity O2 drives up the costs of the process. Other relevant gas mixtures that contain large amounts (40–60 vol %) of CO2 are biogas (produced from the anaerobic digestion of organic matter, such as agricultural waste) and landfill gas (produced from the decomposition of organic waste, such as food waste, in rubbish dumps). (16) The other main component of biogas and landfill gas is methane, which has a global warming potential 28 times larger than carbon dioxide (over a time period of 100 years). (17,18) The energy content of CH4/CO2 gas mixtures depends on the concentration of methane in the gas mixture. For example, the lower heating value (LHV) energy content of methane is 36 MJ m–3CH4 (at STP conditions), while the LHV of biogas with a methane content in the range of 60–65% is approximately 20–25 MJ m–3biogas. (19) By upgrading biogas and landfill gas to biomethane through selective separation of carbon dioxide, a substitute for natural gas is obtained that can be used as a renewable fuel, for example in combined heat and power plants, or as a vehicle fuel. (20) The current biogas and biomethane production potential is 730 million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe), which if fully utilized would cover about 20% of the current worldwide gas demand. (21) However, at this moment, only 35 Mtoe of biogas and biomethane is actually produced. Among the current CO2 separation approaches applied in CCS/CCU and biogas upgrading, absorption in a liquid phase, (22,23) membrane separation, (24,25) and adsorption on solids (26,27) are the most commonly used techniques. Absorption of CO2 in amine solutions is the most mature carbon dioxide capture process and has been used industrially for many years. Introduction Due to the significant environmental and socioeconomic impact of sectors such as construction, there is a growing demand for a paradigm shift aimed at producing increasingly advanced, circular, energy-efficient, and ultimately more sustainable materials (AMI2030, 2022; European Commission, 2023). In this context, the so-called zeolite-geopolymer composites (or geopolymer-zeolite composites) have been attracting increasing attention from the scientific community in the last years. According to Rożek et al. (2019), this hybrid materials combine the advantages of both components, since geopolymer provides mechanical strength and durability, while zeolite contributes with high surface area, porosity, and adsorption capacity. There are three main routes to obtain zeolite-geopolymer composites (Rożek et al., 2019): (1) using zeolites as precursors for geopolymerization, (2) promoting zeolite formation as a parallel reaction during geopolymerization, and (3) applying hydrothermal treatment to previously prepared geopolymers. However, Moreno-Maroto and Alonso-Azcárate (2024) recently proposed a novel approach which could be included alongside the three previous approaches: (4) application of hydrothermal treatment to fired specimens. This new method involves an initial stage of shaping macroscopic pieces, which are fired generally at significantly lower temperatures than those typically used in the ceramics industry and lightweight aggregates (600 °C vs. 900–1300 °C), followed by alkaline hydrothermal treatment. Due to its simplicity and adaptability, it enables the production of materials not only through molding (typical of geopolymers) but also via extrusion, particularly when using clays such as kaolin as precursors, making it more easily adaptable to the ceramic industry. Chemical activation with sodium hydroxide alters zeolite structure and surface by increasing porosity, modifying surface hydroxyl chemistry, and shifting acidity/basicity in a way that can enhance adsorption-related properties. The evidence points to a mechanism centered on alkaline hydrolysis of siliceous zeolite frameworks, where NaOH provides both the hydroxide species and the carrier for water, which together influence desilication and framework modification. In this context, the activated zeolite can develop a more open structure with increased surface area and porosity, while the surface hydroxyl environment changes to create new reactive sites.

On pore structure, the most direct evidence is that alkaline hydrolysis is selective for desilication over dealumination, and that water loading within the pore has a major effect on hydrolysis energetics and mechanism. The cited paper explains that in siliceous zeolites, desilication may be initiated at internal silanol sites, which act as nucleation centers for reactive water, and that nearby Al sites also promote water incorporation into the pore [N1-F1]. This suggests that NaOH activation can open up internal defects and increase the accessibility of pores, which may translate into a more porous framework. The same source also notes that NaOH is present as the carrier of the hydroxide and that the hydrolysis mechanism may involve OH– ions with low reaction barriers, indicating that the activation process can change the pore architecture toward a more mesoporous or hierarchical structure [N1-F1]. Although the evidence does not explicitly quantify pore size or surface area in this direct activation context, it supports the broader idea that NaOH treatment modifies the framework in a way that can increase porosity and surface accessibility.

Regarding surface chemistry, the evidence indicates that NaOH can change surface hydroxyl species. The paper states that SN2 reactions in zeolite ZSM-5 replace framework Si–OSi bonds with Si–OH and SiO–Na+ species, which is a direct example of how NaOH can create new surface hydroxyl groups and cation-associated sites [N1-F1]. It also notes that Na+ can stabilize activated Si complexes at quartz surfaces, implying that the surface becomes richer in hydroxyl-like species and may develop more localized basic sites [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence suggests that NaOH treatment can remove the framework healing route via deprotonation of reaction products, which implies that the surface hydroxyl density and protonation state are altered [N1-F1]. Taken together, this means NaOH activation can increase the number of surface hydroxyl groups and create new basic sites, while also reducing some framework healing or recombination pathways that might otherwise preserve a denser surface.

As for acidity/basicity and active sites, the evidence supports a shift toward more basic surface chemistry. The paper explicitly says that alkaline hydrolysis is selective for desilication over dealumination and that the reaction mechanism is influenced by OH– ions and spectator Na+ cations [N1-F1]. This indicates that the treatment can create a more basic surface environment, which may expose or generate basic sites that are relevant for adsorption. The same source also notes that Na+ can stabilize activated Si complexes and that the cation is likely to affect reaction mechanisms either directly or as a water adsorption center [N1-F1]. This is important because basic sites are often favorable for CO2 adsorption, as CO2 can react with basic surface hydroxyls to form carbonate species [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here is indirect for zeolite activation rather than adsorption, it is consistent with the idea that NaOH treatment increases the density of basic surface sites and active hydroxyl species, which can improve adsorption capacity. The evidence does not provide a direct comparison of acid versus base activation in this specific zeolite activation context, so the conclusion remains that NaOH changes the surface chemistry toward a more hydroxyl-rich, basic framework with new active sites rather than a simple linear increase in acidity [N1-F1].

Overall, NaOH activation changes the zeolite by desilicating the framework, increasing porosity and surface accessibility, creating more hydroxyl and basic sites, and modifying the overall surface hydroxyl chemistry [N1-F1]. These changes are not uniform across all zeolites, because the evidence also notes that pore size and acidity are not generally related, but can depend on framework type and composition [N1-R5]. Therefore, the observed effects are best described as framework-dependent and chemistry-dependent rather than universal.

The evidence suggests that these factors are interdependent and that activation conditions can strongly influence performance.

For optimal NaOH concentration, the evidence indicates that both too low and too high concentrations can be suboptimal. The cited work on natural zeolite activation with 0.5 M and 1.0 M NaOH was discussed, and another study reports that maximum manganese adsorption capacity was achieved with 1.5 M NaOH, with higher concentrations leading to undesirable effects [N5-R2]. This implies that there is an optimal concentration window for surface modification without over-activation. The evidence also shows that alkaline activation can enhance zeolite formation and crystallization, with higher NaOH concentration favoring certain zeolite phases, but also indicating that concentration choice can shape the final material properties [N3-F3]. Therefore, the optimal NaOH concentration is not a single fixed value but depends on the target application and desired surface chemistry.

For time and temperature, the evidence is consistent with the idea that both are critical. The hydrothermal synthesis study reports that zeolitization is enhanced with increasing temperature and NaOH molarity, with zeolite A being predominant at 90 and 120 °C [N3-R2]. It also says that the hydrothermal synthesis of zeolite-geopolymer composites from kaolin-marine plastic aggregates was studied using different temperatures and NaOH concentrations, and that higher temperatures and higher alkalinity enhance precursor solubility, reduce polymerization of silicate species, and accelerate crystallization [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that lower alkaline concentrations combined with higher temperatures favor zeolite A formation, while higher NaOH concentrations can promote other phases [N3-F3]. Taken together, the optimal conditions appear to be a balance between moderate temperature and a sufficient NaOH concentration, with too high a concentration risking over-activation or phase changes that may not be desirable for adsorption. Time is also important because hydrothermal treatment duration affects zeolite crystallization and mineralogical changes, with some studies showing optimal results after 24 h or longer treatment times depending on temperature and concentration [N3-F3]. Thus, the practical use of activated zeolite is enhanced when NaOH concentration, time, and temperature are tuned to the specific target zeolite and application.

Regeneration behavior and stability after multiple cycles are important for practical use. The evidence on regeneration shows that NaOH can be effective for certain adsorbents, such as in the case of a nanocomposite where NaOH was most effective for CR regeneration after five cycles [N6-R1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that activated zeolite can be enhanced by careful control of NaOH concentration, time, and temperature, but practical use is limited by the need to balance activation effectiveness with regeneration stability and environmental impact [N3-F3][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Chemical activation with sodium hydroxide improves zeolite adsorption capacity by altering the material’s structure and surface chemistry in ways that make it more effective for CO2/N2 separation in biogas upgrading. The evidence points to three main mechanisms: it increases porosity and surface accessibility, modifies hydroxyl chemistry to create more reactive sites, and shifts acidity/basicity toward conditions favorable for CO2 adsorption. ### 1) Structural changes: more pores and better accessibility
NaOH activation changes the zeolite framework through alkaline hydrolysis. The evidence explains that alkaline hydrolysis is selective for desilication over dealumination, and that water loading within the pore has a major effect on hydrolysis energetics and mechanism [N1-F1]. This means NaOH treatment can open up internal defects and create a more open framework, which increases porosity and surface accessibility. These structural changes are important because they allow CO2 molecules to reach more active sites and improve the overall surface area available for adsorption.

The evidence further suggests that NaOH can create a more porous, hydroxyl-rich surface by removing framework healing routes and modifying the reaction environment [N1-F1]. While the provided evidence does not directly quantify pore size or surface area for NaOH-activated zeolite, it clearly supports the idea that the activation process can increase porosity and make the material more accessible for adsorption [N1-F1][N1-R5]. This structural change is important for biogas upgrading, where CO2 must be selectively adsorbed from a CH4-rich gas mixture.

### 7) Integrated conclusion
In short, chemical activation with sodium hydroxide improves zeolite adsorption capacity for biogas upgrading by:

- creating a more open framework with increased porosity and surface accessibility [N1-F1][N1-R5],
- modifying surface chemistry to increase the density of hydroxyl groups and basic sites [N1-F1],
- shifting acidity/basicity toward conditions favorable for CO2 adsorption [N1-F1],
- improving CO2/N2 separation capacity and uptake through selective adsorption [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4],
- enhancing kinetic selectivity toward CO2 [N2-R4],
